  if (document.getElementById('tipcard')) return;
  const css = document.createElement('style');
  css.textContent = `
    #tipcard { position: fixed; display: none; max-width: 460px; background: #0a0c0f; border: 1px solid #2a2a2a; border-left: 3px solid #3b82f6; border-radius: 10px; padding: 12px 16px; z-index: 9999; box-shadow: 0 10px 30px rgba(0,0,0,0.65); pointer-events: none; font-family: 'Segoe UI', Roboto, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif; }
    #tipcard .tip-head { color: #3b82f6; font-size: 12px; font-weight: 700; letter-spacing: 0.09em; text-transform: uppercase; margin-bottom: 5px; }
    #tipcard .tip-body { color: #d6d9dc; font-size: 15px; line-height: 1.5; font-weight: 400; }
    body.tips-off #tipcard { display: none !important; }
    body.tips-off [data-tip] { border-bottom-color: transparent !important; text-decoration: none !important; cursor: default !important; }
    #tip-toggle { position: fixed; top: 12px; left: 56px; z-index: 9999; font: 600 12px/1 system-ui, sans-serif; letter-spacing: 0.05em; padding: 7px 14px; border-radius: 999px; border: 1px solid #2a2a2a; background: rgba(17,17,17,0.92); color: #3b82f6; cursor: pointer; opacity: 0.3; transition: opacity 0.15s ease; }
    #tip-toggle:hover { opacity: 1; }
    #tip-toggle.tips-off { text-decoration: line-through; }
    @media print { #tip-toggle { display: none !important; } }`;
  document.head.appendChild(css);
  const card = document.createElement('div');
  card.id = 'tipcard';
  card.innerHTML = '<div class="tip-head"></div><div class="tip-body"></div>';
  document.body.appendChild(card);
  const btn = document.createElement('button');
  btn.id = 'tip-toggle'; btn.type = 'button'; btn.textContent = 'Tips';
  btn.title = 'Hover tooltips are on — click to disable';
  btn.addEventListener('click', () => {
    const off = document.body.classList.toggle('tips-off');
    btn.classList.toggle('tips-off', off);
    btn.textContent = off ? 'Tips off' : 'Tips';
    btn.title = off ? 'Hover tooltips are off — click to enable' : 'Hover tooltips are on — click to disable';
  });
  document.body.appendChild(btn);
  const head = card.firstChild, body = card.lastChild;
  const place = (ev) => {
    const pad = 16, r = card.getBoundingClientRect();
    let x = ev.clientX + pad, y = ev.clientY + pad;
    if (x + r.width > innerWidth - 10) x = ev.clientX - r.width - pad;
    if (y + r.height > innerHeight - 10) y = ev.clientY - r.height - pad;
    card.style.left = Math.max(8, x) + 'px'; card.style.top = Math.max(8, y) + 'px';
  };
  document.addEventListener('mousemove', (ev) => {
    const t = ev.target.closest && ev.target.closest('[data-tip]');
    if (t) {
      head.textContent = t.getAttribute('data-tiphead') || 'Explanation';
      body.textContent = t.getAttribute('data-tip');
      card.style.display = 'block';
      place(ev);
    } else {
      card.style.display = 'none';
    }
  });
})();
</script>

# **Vaswani et al. (2017):** Attention Is All You Need

## Drop recurrence entirely and every word reads every other in one hop: **28.4 BLEU** after 3.5 days on 8 GPUs

<p class="byline">Google Brain, Google Research, University of Toronto · NIPS 2017, arXiv June 2017</p>

<p class="links"><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762">arXiv</a><a href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.03762v7">PDF</a><a href="https://papers.nips.cc/paper_files/paper/2017/hash/3f5ee243547dee91fbd053c1c4a845aa-Abstract.html">NIPS proceedings</a><a href="https://github.com/tensorflow/tensor2tensor">code (tensor2tensor)</a><a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762">section anchors</a></p>

---

<a class="slide-id" id="d142f4eb-5bea-4ed1-925d-d5c2ef7023bd"></a>

## TL;DR

<div class="columns-wide-left" style="grid-template-columns: 64% 36%; gap: 28px; align-items: start">
<div>

- **What it is** — the **Transformer**: translation built **only from attention**, with **no recurrence and no convolution** anywhere.
- **The trick** — **every position reads every other position in one step**, so any two words sit <span class="term" data-tiphead="One hop, not n" data-tip="n is the sentence length in tokens. A recurrent model carries information from word 1 to word n through n steps; one self-attention layer connects them directly. Table 1 calls this the maximum path length, slide 20.">**one hop apart, not n**</span>.
- **The stabilisers** — scores divided by <span class="term" data-tiphead="Square root of d_k" data-tip="d_k is the width of each query and key vector, 64 in the base model. Dividing the attention scores by its square root keeps the softmax out of its flat, saturated region; slide 15.">**√d_k**</span>, a <span class="term" data-tiphead="Residual + LayerNorm wrapper" data-tip="Each sub-layer adds its input back to its output (the residual) and then normalises the sum per position (LayerNorm); slide 18 shows it.">**residual + LayerNorm** wrapper</span> on every sub-layer, and a <span class="term" data-tiphead="Warmup, then inverse-sqrt decay" data-tip="The learning rate rises linearly for the first 4000 training steps, then falls as one over the square root of the step number; slide 22.">**warmup then inverse-sqrt** learning-rate decay</span>.
- **The numbers** — the <span class="term" data-tiphead="Base and big" data-tip="The paper trains two sizes. Base: 6 layers, width 512, 8 heads, 65M parameters. Big: width 1024, 16 heads, 213M parameters. Slide 21 lists both.">**big** model</span> scores <span class="term" data-tiphead="BLEU" data-tip="A precision-style score comparing machine output to human reference translations by counting matching word n-grams, with a penalty for output that is too short. Higher is better; one BLEU point is a large gap on WMT.">**28.4 BLEU**</span> (n-gram overlap with reference translations, 0–100) English-German on newstest2014 as a **single model**, **over 2 BLEU** past the previous best, an **ensemble** of ConvS2S models at 26.36 — after **3.5 days on 8 <span class="term" data-tiphead="P100" data-tip="NVIDIA Tesla P100, a 2016 data-centre GPU. For its cost estimates the paper assumes 9.5 TFLOPS of sustained single-precision throughput per P100.">P100s</span>**; **41.8** English-French (§6.1's text says 41.0); the **base** model gets 27.3 in **12 hours**.
- **Why it mattered** — BERT, GPT and every LLM since are **built from halves of this one diagram**.

</div>
<div style="text-align:center">
<span style="position:relative; display:inline-block"><img src="images/paper/fig1-architecture.png" style="height:430px; width:auto; border-radius:6px"/><span data-tiphead="Encoder, left stack" data-tip="Six identical layers: multi-head self-attention, then a position-wise feed-forward network, each wrapped in Add and Norm. BERT keeps this half." style="position:absolute; left:8%; top:36%; width:40%; height:38%"></span><span data-tiphead="Decoder, right stack" data-tip="Six identical layers with a third sub-layer in the middle that attends over the encoder output; the first sub-layer is masked so position i never reads a later position. GPT keeps this half, minus the middle sub-layer." style="position:absolute; left:52%; top:20%; width:40%; height:54%"></span></span>

<!-- _class: fs-sm -->

## The task is machine translation: English in, German or French out

- **Machine translation** on the WMT 2014 benchmarks: **English→German** (about 4.5M sentence pairs) and **English→French** (36M sentences); every headline number is a **BLEU** score on newstest2014 (§5.1, §6.1)
- **One sentence, step by step** (illustrative, **not model output**): the encoder reads the **whole English sentence at once**; the decoder writes German **one token per step**, each step reading the source words it needs

---

<a class="slide-id" id="b3eefbd1-c4fd-4725-a2dd-2a41e953f300"></a>

## The core idea — every word reads every other directly

- **Why care:** recurrence **ties positions to steps in computation time** — no parallelism inside a sentence.
- **What prior work does:** ByteNet and ConvS2S use convolutions, but relating two positions takes **more operations the further apart they are** — linearly for ConvS2S, logarithmically for ByteNet (§2).
- **What this paper does instead:** one layer relates **every pair of positions in a constant number of sequential operations**, however far apart.
- **The enabling fact:** attention already sat inside recurrent <span class="term" data-tiphead="Encoder-decoder" data-tip="An encoder turns the whole input sentence into one vector per token; a decoder then writes the output one token at a time. Attention lets each decoder step look back at the encoder vectors it needs instead of one fixed summary.">encoder-decoders</span> — this paper **keeps it and deletes the recurrence**.
- **Lifted from:** self-attention existed for reading comprehension; this is **the first <span class="term" data-tiphead="Transduction" data-tip="Mapping one sequence to another sequence, possibly of a different length, such as an English sentence to a German one.">transduction</span> model built only on it**.

---

<a class="slide-id" id="660bc4a6-fdf8-4f62-8d79-4655ed122775"></a>

<!-- _class: fs-sm -->

## The five Cs, in one look

Five Cs — a standard first-pass checklist for a paper: Category, Context, Correctness, Contributions, Clarity.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Category** | An **architecture paper** with one ablation table (Table 3) over heads, key size, model size, dropout, label smoothing and positions. |
| **Context** | Displaces recurrent ([GNMT](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.08144)) and convolutional seq2seq ([ConvS2S](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.03122), [ByteNet](https://arxiv.org/abs/1610.10099)); attention itself is [Bahdanau et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.0473) |
| **Correctness** | Quality rests on **two test sets, single runs, no error bars**; cost rests on **estimated** FLOPs. |
| **Contributions** | Scaled dot-product and multi-head attention, a purely attentional encoder-decoder, **state of the art on both language pairs**; the **base** model beats every English-German baseline **at a fraction of their estimated cost**. |
| **Clarity** | [Figure 1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.F1) and [Table 1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S4.T1) carry the argument; §3.2.3, the three uses of attention (slide 12), is the paragraph everyone re-reads. |

---

<a class="slide-id" id="c8eed2f7-be48-4290-9095-5e3f550d9367"></a>

<!-- _class: fs-lg -->

## Should you read further?

- **Read §3, the model, and §6, the results, if** you work on anything sequence-shaped — this is the architecture under BERT, GPT and every LLM in production; the mechanism is on **slides 8–20**, the evidence on **slides 24–27**.
- **Skim §3.2, the attention section, and Figure 2 if** you only need **what Q, K and V are** and **why the scores are divided by √d_k** — two pages and one figure, walked through on **slides 11–17**.
- **Skip it if** you want long-context or efficiency work: the O(n²) cost is acknowledged here only as future work (**slide 20**), and lives in [FlashAttention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14135) and [Longformer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.05150) instead.

---

<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS1" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Output z_1" data-tip="Every output position is a weighted sum over all input positions, so it depends on the whole sequence but on no other output.">
<rect x="621" y="108" width="80" height="54" rx="9" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#20304a" stroke-width="2"/>
<rect class="whyn-z0" x="621" y="108" width="80" height="54" rx="9" fill="#3b82f6" fill-opacity=".18" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="2.2" opacity="1"/>

</a>

</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS1" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Output z_3" data-tip="Serialisation moves from the sequence axis to the depth axis: N = 6 layers, not n positions.">
<rect x="825" y="108" width="80" height="54" rx="9" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#20304a" stroke-width="2"/>
<rect class="whyn-z2" x="825" y="108" width="80" height="54" rx="9" fill="#3b82f6" fill-opacity=".18" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="2.2" opacity="1"/>
<text x="865" y="141" text-anchor="middle" class="whyn-m whyn-t" font-size="16">z_3</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS1" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Output z_4" data-tip="Order is not implied by the computation at all, which is exactly why positional encodings have to be added at the bottom of the stack.">
<rect x="927" y="108" width="80" height="54" rx="9" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#20304a" stroke-width="2"/>
<rect class="whyn-z3" x="927" y="108" width="80" height="54" rx="9" fill="#3b82f6" fill-opacity=".18" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="2.2" opacity="1"/>
<text x="967" y="141" text-anchor="middle" class="whyn-m whyn-t" font-size="16">z_4</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS1" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Output z_5" data-tip="The last position is one hop from the first, which is the O(1) maximum path length of Table 1.">
<rect x="1029" y="108" width="80" height="54" rx="9" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#20304a" stroke-width="2"/>
<rect class="whyn-z4" x="1029" y="108" width="80" height="54" rx="9" fill="#3b82f6" fill-opacity=".18" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="2.2" opacity="1"/>
<text x="1069" y="141" text-anchor="middle" class="whyn-m whyn-t" font-size="16">z_5</text>
</a>
<text x="632" y="286" class="whyn-d" font-size="12.5">every z reads every x in one sub-layer; no z waits for another z</text>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S1" target="_blank" data-tiphead="The cost of recurrence" data-tip="The introduction names this as the fundamental constraint: aligning positions to steps in computation time precludes parallelization within training examples.">
<rect x="40" y="320" width="530" height="100" rx="10" fill="#151515" stroke="#4a3520" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="64" y="346" fill="#f0883e" font-size="14.5" font-weight="700">O(n) sequential operations</text>
<text x="64" y="370" class="whyn-d" font-size="12.5">The paper: this inherently sequential nature precludes</text>
<text x="64" y="390" class="whyn-d" font-size="12.5">parallelization within training examples, which becomes</text>
<text x="64" y="410" class="whyn-d" font-size="12.5">critical at longer sequence lengths.</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S4" target="_blank" data-tiphead="What attention buys" data-tip="Table 1 gives a self-attention layer a constant number of sequentially executed operations, against O(n) for a recurrent layer.">
<rect x="610" y="320" width="510" height="100" rx="10" fill="#151515" stroke="#20304a" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="634" y="346" fill="#3b82f6" font-size="14.5" font-weight="700">O(1) sequential operations</text>
<text x="634" y="370" class="whyn-d" font-size="12.5">In training, and always in the encoder, every position is</text>
<text x="634" y="390" class="whyn-d" font-size="12.5">computed in the same step: long sentences add no sequential</text>
<text x="634" y="410" class="whyn-d" font-size="12.5">steps. At inference the decoder still writes one token per step.</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S4" target="_blank" data-tiphead="The trade" data-tip="Self-attention buys parallelism and short paths, and pays for them with a cost that is quadratic in the sequence length. The paper argues that is the right side of the trade for sentence-length inputs.">
<rect x="40" y="442" width="1080" height="140" rx="10" fill="#0d1117" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="1.8"/>
<text x="64" y="470" class="whyn-t" font-size="15">The trade the paper is making</text>
<text x="64" y="498" class="whyn-d" font-size="13">Win: a new state of the art in translation quality after training for as little as twelve hours on eight P100 GPUs.</text>
<text x="64" y="520" class="whyn-d" font-size="13">Cost per layer (Table 1): self-attention scores all n x n pairs, each a d-wide dot product: O(n^2 . d). A recurrent layer</text>
<text x="64" y="542" class="whyn-d" font-size="13">runs n steps, each a d x d matrix times a vector: O(n . d^2). Here d is the model width d_model = 512, not the 64-wide d_k.</text>
<text x="64" y="564" class="whyn-d" font-size="13">So attention is the cheaper layer while sentence length n stays below 512; the paper says this is "most often" so, but quotes no lengths.</text>
</a>
</svg>
</div>

<text x="132" y="416" class="arch-d" font-size="11" text-anchor="end">residual</text>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS2.SSS3" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Encoder self-attention" data-tip="All three inputs come from one place: the output of the previous encoder layer. Q, K and V are three different learned linear projections of that same matrix, so every position may attend to every position of the layer below it.">
<rect x="170" y="402" width="260" height="48" rx="9" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="300" y="422" text-anchor="middle" class="arch-t" font-size="15.5">Multi-Head Attention</text>
<text x="300" y="440" text-anchor="middle" class="arch-m" font-size="11">Q, K, V: encoder layer below</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS1" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Add and Norm" data-tip="A residual connection adds the sub-layer input back to its output, then layer normalisation rescales it. The paper writes this as LayerNorm of x plus Sublayer of x. Every sub-layer and every embedding emits 512 dimensions so the addition is always shape-compatible.">
<rect x="170" y="356" width="260" height="32" rx="8" fill="#141414" stroke="#20304a" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="300" y="377" text-anchor="middle" class="arch-d" font-size="13">Add &amp; Norm</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS3" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Position-wise feed-forward" data-tip="Two linear layers with a ReLU between them, applied to each position separately and identically. Inner width is 2048, outer width 512. Same weights across positions inside one layer, different weights in every layer.">
<rect x="170" y="294" width="260" height="48" rx="9" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#3fb950" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="300" y="314" text-anchor="middle" class="arch-t" font-size="15.5">Feed Forward</text>
<text x="300" y="332" text-anchor="middle" class="arch-m" font-size="11">512 -&gt; 2048 -&gt; 512</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS1" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Add and Norm" data-tip="The second residual plus layer-norm of the encoder layer, wrapped around the feed-forward sub-layer. Dropout with rate 0.1 is applied to the sub-layer output before the addition.">
<rect x="170" y="248" width="260" height="32" rx="8" fill="#141414" stroke="#20304a" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="300" y="269" text-anchor="middle" class="arch-d" font-size="13">Add &amp; Norm</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS4" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Input embedding" data-tip="A learned lookup table turning each byte-pair token id into a 512-dimensional vector. Its weight matrix is shared with the output embedding and with the pre-softmax linear layer, and is multiplied by the square root of 512.">
<rect x="170" y="504" width="260" height="48" rx="9" fill="#0d1117" stroke="#2a2a2a" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="300" y="524" text-anchor="middle" class="arch-t" font-size="14.5">Input Embedding</text>
<text x="300" y="542" text-anchor="middle" class="arch-m" font-size="10.5">token ids to 512-dim</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS2.SSS3" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Masked decoder self-attention" data-tip="All three inputs come from the output of the previous decoder layer, but every score for a future position is set to minus infinity before the softmax, so position i can only see positions up to and including i.">
<rect x="630" y="402" width="300" height="48" rx="9" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#f0883e" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="780" y="422" text-anchor="middle" class="arch-t" font-size="15.5">Masked Multi-Head Attention</text>
<text x="780" y="440" text-anchor="middle" class="arch-m" font-size="11">Q, K, V: decoder layer below</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS1" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Add and Norm" data-tip="Residual plus layer normalisation around the masked self-attention sub-layer of the decoder.">
<rect x="630" y="356" width="300" height="32" rx="8" fill="#141414" stroke="#20304a" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="780" y="377" text-anchor="middle" class="arch-d" font-size="13">Add &amp; Norm</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS2.SSS3" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Encoder-decoder attention" data-tip="The only place where the two stacks meet. Queries come from the previous decoder layer; keys and values come from the output of the encoder stack, meaning its final layer, and the same encoder output feeds this sub-layer in all six decoder layers. Every decoder position can attend over every input position.">
<rect x="630" y="294" width="300" height="48" rx="9" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#bc8cff" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="780" y="314" text-anchor="middle" class="arch-t" font-size="15.5">Multi-Head Attention</text>
<text x="780" y="332" text-anchor="middle" class="arch-m" font-size="11">Q: decoder | K, V: encoder</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS1" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Add and Norm" data-tip="Residual plus layer normalisation around the encoder-decoder attention sub-layer.">
<rect x="630" y="248" width="300" height="32" rx="8" fill="#141414" stroke="#20304a" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="780" y="269" text-anchor="middle" class="arch-d" font-size="13">Add &amp; Norm</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS3" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Position-wise feed-forward" data-tip="Identical in form to the encoder feed-forward sub-layer: 512 in, 2048 hidden with ReLU, 512 out, applied at each position independently.">
<rect x="630" y="186" width="300" height="48" rx="9" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#3fb950" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="780" y="206" text-anchor="middle" class="arch-t" font-size="15.5">Feed Forward</text>
<text x="780" y="224" text-anchor="middle" class="arch-m" font-size="11">512 -&gt; 2048 -&gt; 512</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS1" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Add and Norm" data-tip="Residual plus layer normalisation around the decoder feed-forward sub-layer. This is the third such wrapper in every decoder layer, against two in every encoder layer.">
<rect x="630" y="140" width="300" height="32" rx="8" fill="#141414" stroke="#20304a" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="780" y="161" text-anchor="middle" class="arch-d" font-size="13">Add &amp; Norm</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS4" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Output embedding" data-tip="The same kind of lookup table as on the encoder side, applied to the tokens generated so far. The sequence is offset by one position so that the prediction for position i never consumes the token at position i.">
<rect x="630" y="504" width="300" height="48" rx="9" fill="#0d1117" stroke="#2a2a2a" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="780" y="524" text-anchor="middle" class="arch-t" font-size="14.5">Output Embedding</text>
<text x="780" y="542" text-anchor="middle" class="arch-m" font-size="10.5">shifted right by one</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS4" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Linear projection" data-tip="Projects the 512-dimensional decoder output onto the vocabulary. Its weight matrix is tied to both embedding tables, which is why the same matrix appears three times in the model.">
<rect x="690" y="62" width="180" height="38" rx="9" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#93c5fd" stroke-width="1.8"/>
<text x="780" y="86" text-anchor="middle" class="arch-t" font-size="15">Linear</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS4" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Softmax" data-tip="Turns vocabulary logits into next-token probabilities. At inference the model is decoded with beam search of width 4 and length penalty 0.6.">
<rect x="690" y="8" width="180" height="38" rx="9" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#93c5fd" stroke-width="1.8"/>
<text x="780" y="32" text-anchor="middle" class="arch-t" font-size="15">Softmax</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS5" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Positional encoding" data-tip="Fixed sine and cosine waves of geometrically spaced wavelengths, added to the embeddings. Without them the model has no notion of order at all, because attention is a set operation.">
<rect x="20" y="452" width="125" height="52" rx="9" fill="#0d1117" stroke="#666" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="82" y="474" text-anchor="middle" class="arch-d" font-size="13">Positional</text>
<text x="82" y="492" text-anchor="middle" class="arch-d" font-size="13">Encoding</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS5" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Positional encoding" data-tip="The same fixed sinusoids are added at the bottom of the decoder stack. They are parameter-free, so nothing about position has to be learned.">
<rect x="1015" y="452" width="125" height="52" rx="9" fill="#0d1117" stroke="#666" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="1077" y="474" text-anchor="middle" class="arch-d" font-size="13">Positional</text>
<text x="1077" y="492" text-anchor="middle" class="arch-d" font-size="13">Encoding</text>
</a>
<circle cx="300" cy="478" r="12" fill="#111111" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="2"/>
<circle cx="780" cy="478" r="12" fill="#111111" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="300" y="483" text-anchor="middle" fill="#3b82f6" font-size="15" font-weight="700">+</text>
<text x="780" y="483" text-anchor="middle" fill="#3b82f6" font-size="15" font-weight="700">+</text>
<text x="300" y="576" text-anchor="middle" class="arch-d" font-size="13">source tokens</text>
<text x="780" y="576" text-anchor="middle" class="arch-d" font-size="13">tokens generated so far</text>
<text x="905" y="31" class="arch-d" font-size="12.5">next-token probabilities</text>
</svg>
</div>

- **Encoder layer**: self-attention + <span class="term" data-tiphead="Position-wise feed-forward network" data-tip="Two linear layers with a ReLU between them, applied to every position separately and with the same weights inside one layer. It mixes the channels of one token, never two tokens.">feed-forward</span>; each **decoder** layer adds a third sub-layer that reads the **final** encoder layer's output — the same keys and values in all six
- Every sub-layer is wrapped in <span class="term" data-tiphead="Residual connection" data-tip="The sub-layer input is added back to its output before normalisation, so a layer only has to learn a correction to what it received rather than a full replacement.">residual</span> + <span class="term" data-tiphead="Layer normalisation" data-tip="Rescales each position vector to zero mean and unit variance across its own features, then applies a learned gain and bias. Unlike batch norm it does not look at other examples.">LayerNorm</span>, so every sub-layer and embedding reads and writes 512-wide vectors

<text x="684" y="400" class="tf-d" font-size="13">Each step runs the decoder again and feeds the</text>
<text x="684" y="420" class="tf-d" font-size="13">new token back in. The paper: at each step the</text>
<text x="684" y="440" class="tf-d" font-size="13">model consumes the previously generated symbols</text>
<text x="684" y="460" class="tf-d" font-size="13">as additional input when generating the next.</text>
<text x="684" y="500" fill="#f0f0f0" font-size="13" font-weight="700">So decoding stays sequential in the output length;</text>
<text x="684" y="520" fill="#f0f0f0" font-size="13" font-weight="700">the one-pass shortcut exists only in training,</text>
<text x="684" y="540" fill="#f0f0f0" font-size="13" font-weight="700">where the reference translation is known.</text>
</a>
<text x="1136" y="576" text-anchor="end" fill="#f0883e" font-size="11.5">German tokens illustrative; &lt;s&gt; marks the start of the output</text>
</svg>

- **Shifted right by one** (§3.1): decoder input i holds reference token i−1 and must predict token i
- **Teacher forcing** (standard name, not the paper's): feed the **reference**, not the model's guesses, so **all positions train in one pass**
- **A causal mask** (slide 17) lets position i read only inputs 1…i, reference tokens up to i−1 — never the token it must predict

---

<a class="slide-id" id="cd7035fc-fa18-480d-bde4-eb7645fe7d95"></a>

<text x="70" y="486" class="flow-d" font-size="12.5">top row: what the decoder has so far, starting from &lt;s&gt;; bottom row: the German it has written</text>
<text class="flow-st0" opacity="0" x="70" y="520" font-size="14" font-weight="700" fill="#f0f0f0">Decoder step 1 of 6: writing <tspan fill="#3fb950">Das</tspan>, reading mostly <tspan fill="#bc8cff">The</tspan></text>
<text class="flow-st1" opacity="0" x="70" y="520" font-size="14" font-weight="700" fill="#f0f0f0">Decoder step 2 of 6: writing <tspan fill="#3fb950">Gesetz</tspan>, reading mostly <tspan fill="#bc8cff">law</tspan></text>
<text class="flow-st2" opacity="1" x="70" y="520" font-size="14" font-weight="700" fill="#f0f0f0">Decoder step 3 of 6: writing <tspan fill="#3fb950">wird</tspan>, reading mostly <tspan fill="#bc8cff">will</tspan></text>
<text class="flow-st3" opacity="0" x="70" y="520" font-size="14" font-weight="700" fill="#f0f0f0">Decoder step 4 of 6: writing <tspan fill="#3fb950">nie</tspan>, reading mostly <tspan fill="#bc8cff">never</tspan></text>
<text class="flow-st4" opacity="0" x="70" y="520" font-size="14" font-weight="700" fill="#f0f0f0">Decoder step 5 of 6: writing <tspan fill="#3fb950">perfekt</tspan>, reading mostly <tspan fill="#bc8cff">perfect</tspan></text>
<text class="flow-st5" opacity="0" x="70" y="520" font-size="14" font-weight="700" fill="#f0f0f0">Decoder step 6 of 6: writing <tspan fill="#3fb950">sein</tspan>, reading mostly <tspan fill="#bc8cff">be</tspan></text>
<text class="flow-st-f" opacity="0" x="70" y="520" font-size="14" font-weight="700" fill="#f0f0f0">Done: six steps for six German words, one encoder pass</text>
<text class="flow-st-e" opacity="0" x="70" y="520" font-size="14" font-weight="700" fill="#f0f0f0">Encoder: one step for all six English words</text>
<text x="70" y="552" fill="#f0883e" font-size="11.5">Illustrative: the German words and attention strengths are not from the paper. One layer and one of eight heads shown;</text>
<text x="70" y="570" fill="#f0883e" font-size="11.5">the model stacks six encoder and six decoder layers and decodes with beam search over 4 candidates, not one greedy word.</text>
<rect x="858" y="14" width="282" height="572" rx="12" fill="#0d1117" stroke="#2a2a2a" stroke-width="1.4"/>
<text x="878" y="44" class="flow-d" font-size="12" font-weight="700" letter-spacing=".08em">WHAT HAPPENS, IN ORDER</text>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS2.SSS3" target="_blank" class="flow-lg0" data-tiphead="Encoder self-attention, one sentence" data-tip="Keys, values and queries all come from the previous encoder layer, so each position attends to all positions of the layer below. The encoder maps the sentence to one vector per word; given those, the decoder then generates the output one word at a time.">
<rect x="870" y="70" width="258" height="132" rx="9" fill="#141414" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<circle cx="892" cy="90" r="11" fill="#3b82f6"/><text x="892" y="95" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#0d1117">1</text>
<text x="910" y="95" font-size="14" font-weight="700" fill="#3b82f6">Encoder self-attention</text>
<text x="882" y="120" class="flow-d" font-size="12.5">Every English word looks at every</text>
<text x="882" y="138" class="flow-d" font-size="12.5">English word, all six at once. Out</text>
<text x="882" y="156" class="flow-d" font-size="12.5">comes one vector per word (The',</text>
<text x="882" y="174" class="flow-d" font-size="12.5">law', ...), kept for the whole</text>
<text x="882" y="192" class="flow-d" font-size="12.5">translation.</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS2.SSS3" target="_blank" class="flow-lg1" data-tiphead="Masked self-attention, one step" data-tip="Each decoder position attends to all decoder positions up to and including itself. In training a mask sets the scores of later positions to minus infinity; when generating, later words do not exist yet.">
<rect x="870" y="216" width="258" height="96" rx="9" fill="#141414" stroke="#f0883e" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<circle cx="892" cy="236" r="11" fill="#f0883e"/><text x="892" y="241" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#0d1117">2</text>
<text x="910" y="241" font-size="14" font-weight="700" fill="#f0883e">Masked self-attention</text>
<text x="882" y="266" class="flow-d" font-size="12.5">The decoder's newest position looks</text>
<text x="882" y="284" class="flow-d" font-size="12.5">at the German written so far, itself</text>
<text x="882" y="302" class="flow-d" font-size="12.5">included, never ahead.</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS2.SSS3" target="_blank" class="flow-lg2" data-tiphead="Encoder-decoder attention, one step" data-tip="Queries come from the previous decoder layer; keys and values come from the output of the encoder, so every decoder position can attend over all positions of the English sentence.">
<rect x="870" y="326" width="258" height="114" rx="9" fill="#141414" stroke="#bc8cff" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<circle cx="892" cy="346" r="11" fill="#bc8cff"/><text x="892" y="351" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#0d1117">3</text>
<text x="910" y="351" font-size="14" font-weight="700" fill="#bc8cff">Encoder-decoder attention</text>
<text x="882" y="376" class="flow-d" font-size="12.5">Its query searches the encoder</text>
<text x="882" y="394" class="flow-d" font-size="12.5">output for what to translate next.</text>
<text x="882" y="412" class="flow-d" font-size="12.5">Thick line: the English word it</text>
<text x="882" y="430" class="flow-d" font-size="12.5">reads most, into the word written.</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3" target="_blank" class="flow-lg3" data-tiphead="Next word, fed back" data-tip="The model is auto-regressive: at each step it consumes the previously generated symbols as additional input when generating the next. The paper decodes with beam search of size 4 rather than one greedy word.">
<rect x="870" y="454" width="258" height="96" rx="9" fill="#141414" stroke="#3fb950" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<circle cx="892" cy="474" r="11" fill="#3fb950"/><text x="892" y="479" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#0d1117">4</text>
<text x="910" y="479" font-size="14" font-weight="700" fill="#3fb950">Next word</text>
<text x="882" y="504" class="flow-d" font-size="12.5">It writes one German word, which</text>
<text x="882" y="522" class="flow-d" font-size="12.5">is fed back in as the next input.</text>
<text x="882" y="540" class="flow-d" font-size="12.5">Repeat until the sentence is done.</text>
</a>
</svg>
</div>

- **At inference** the encoder runs once; each step feeds the tokens so far back into the decoder, and beam search extends **4 candidate prefixes** at a time. How earlier steps are reused the paper does not say; implementations cache each layer's keys and values

- A **query** asks, a **key** advertises, a **value** is what gets copied out — so a position can advertise one thing and deliver another
- **All three are learned projections**, per **head** i (one of 8 parallel lookups, slide 16): `X W_i^Q`, `Y W_i^K`, `Y W_i^V`, with **X the reading positions** and **Y the positions read**; X = Y except in encoder-decoder attention (next slide). Equation 1's Q, K, V are these projected matrices

<text x="955" y="86" text-anchor="middle" class="qkvt-d" font-size="11.5">Sec 3.2.3, first bullet</text>
</a>
<a class="qkvt-p0" href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS2.SSS3" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Where Q comes from" data-tip="The encoder has no external source to query: the queries are a projection of the layer below, exactly like the keys and values.">
<rect x="35" y="112" width="340" height="56" rx="9" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#20304a" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="57" y="136" class="qkvt-t" font-size="14"><tspan class="qkvt-m" fill="#3b82f6" font-size="15">Q</tspan><tspan dx="12">from the previous encoder layer</tspan></text>
<text x="57" y="156" class="qkvt-d" font-size="11.5">layer 1 sees embeddings plus positional encoding</text>
</a>
<a class="qkvt-p0" href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS2.SSS3" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Where K and V come from" data-tip="The paper states it plainly: in a self-attention layer all of the keys, values and queries come from the same place, the output of the previous layer in the encoder.">
<rect x="35" y="178" width="340" height="56" rx="9" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#20304a" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="57" y="202" class="qkvt-t" font-size="14"><tspan class="qkvt-m" fill="#3b82f6" font-size="15">K, V</tspan><tspan dx="12">from the same previous layer</tspan></text>
<text x="57" y="222" class="qkvt-d" font-size="11.5">same tensor as Q, three different projection matrices</text>
</a>
<a class="qkvt-p1" href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS2.SSS3" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Where Q comes from" data-tip="A projection of the decoder representation of the token being predicted. Under teacher forcing the whole target sequence is present at once, which is why a mask is needed at all.">
<rect x="410" y="112" width="340" height="56" rx="9" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#4a3520" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="432" y="136" class="qkvt-t" font-size="14"><tspan class="qkvt-m" fill="#f0883e" font-size="15">Q</tspan><tspan dx="12">from the previous decoder layer</tspan></text>
<text x="432" y="156" class="qkvt-d" font-size="11.5">one query per target position generated so far</text>
</a>
<a class="qkvt-p1" href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS2.SSS3" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Where K and V come from" data-tip="Also the previous decoder layer. The restriction to positions up to and including i is imposed by the mask inside scaled dot-product attention, not by where the tensors come from.">
<rect x="410" y="178" width="340" height="56" rx="9" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#4a3520" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="432" y="202" class="qkvt-t" font-size="14"><tspan class="qkvt-m" fill="#f0883e" font-size="15">K, V</tspan><tspan dx="12">from the same previous layer</tspan></text>
<text x="432" y="222" class="qkvt-d" font-size="11.5">the mask, not the source, is what makes it causal</text>
</a>
<a class="qkvt-p2" href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS2.SSS3" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Where Q comes from" data-tip="The queries come from the previous decoder layer, so the target side decides what to look for in the source sentence.">
<rect x="785" y="112" width="340" height="56" rx="9" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#3d2f52" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="807" y="136" class="qkvt-t" font-size="14"><tspan class="qkvt-m" fill="#bc8cff" font-size="15">Q</tspan><tspan dx="12">from the previous decoder layer</tspan></text>
<text x="807" y="156" class="qkvt-d" font-size="11.5">the target side asks the question</text>
</a>
<a class="qkvt-p2" href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS2.SSS3" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Where K and V come from" data-tip="The memory keys and values come from the output of the encoder stack, computed once for the whole source sentence and reused at every decoder layer and every decoding step.">
<rect x="785" y="178" width="340" height="56" rx="9" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#3d2f52" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="807" y="202" class="qkvt-t" font-size="14"><tspan class="qkvt-m" fill="#bc8cff" font-size="15">K, V</tspan><tspan dx="12">from the encoder stack output</tspan></text>
<text x="807" y="222" class="qkvt-d" font-size="11.5">the source side supplies the answer</text>
</a>

<text x="42" y="452" class="qkvt-p0 qkvt-t" font-size="12.5">Every position attends to every position of the</text>

## Equation 1 is four operations, and every symbol has a job

<div style="display:flex;justify-content:center;margin-top:0.2rem">
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 1160 600" width="860" height="445" style="max-width:100%" font-family="Inter, sans-serif">
<style>.scal-t{fill:#f0f0f0;font-weight:700}.scal-m{font-family:'JetBrains Mono',monospace}.scal-d{fill:#a0a0a0}.scal-hd{fill:#3b82f6;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.06em}</style>
<defs>
<marker id="ag" markerWidth="11" markerHeight="11" refX="8" refY="4" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4 L0,8 z" fill="#3b82f6"/></marker>
<marker id="av" markerWidth="11" markerHeight="11" refX="8" refY="4" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4 L0,8 z" fill="#bc8cff"/></marker>
</defs>
<rect x="0" y="0" width="1160" height="600" fill="#111111"/>
<text x="258" y="96" text-anchor="middle" class="scal-hd" font-size="15">Scaled Dot-Product Attention</text>
<text x="258" y="114" text-anchor="middle" class="scal-d" font-size="11.5">Figure 2, left panel, redrawn</text>
<path d="M148,536 L148,508" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="2.2" marker-end="url(#ag)" fill="none"/>
<path d="M238,536 L238,508" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="2.2" marker-end="url(#ag)" fill="none"/>
<path d="M193,460 L193,444" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="2.2" marker-end="url(#ag)" fill="none"/>
<path d="M193,396 L193,380" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="2.2" marker-end="url(#ag)" fill="none"/>
<path d="M193,332 L193,316" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="2.2" marker-end="url(#ag)" fill="none"/>
<path d="M193,268 L193,244" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="2.2" marker-end="url(#ag)" fill="none"/>
<path d="M258,196 L258,174" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="2.2" marker-end="url(#ag)" fill="none"/>
<path d="M368,536 L368,244" stroke="#bc8cff" stroke-width="2.2" marker-end="url(#av)" fill="none"/>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS2.SSS3" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Q, the queries" data-tip="One row per position that is doing the looking. Each row is a learned linear projection of that position s current representation, of width d_k = 64 inside a head.">
<rect x="110" y="536" width="76" height="36" rx="8" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="148" y="560" text-anchor="middle" class="scal-t" font-size="17">Q</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS2.SSS3" target="_blank" data-tiphead="K, the keys" data-tip="One row per position that can be looked at. A key is the advertisement a position offers: the query is compared against it to decide how much attention that position gets.">
<rect x="200" y="536" width="76" height="36" rx="8" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="238" y="560" text-anchor="middle" class="scal-t" font-size="17">K</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS2.SSS3" target="_blank" data-tiphead="V, the values" data-tip="The content that actually gets read out and summed. Values have width d_v, which the paper sets equal to d_k = 64. Keys decide how much, values decide what.">
<rect x="330" y="536" width="76" height="36" rx="8" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#bc8cff" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="368" y="560" text-anchor="middle" class="scal-t" font-size="17">V</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.E1" target="_blank" data-tiphead="MatMul: Q times K transposed" data-tip="One dot product per query-key pair. With n positions the result is an n by n matrix of raw compatibility scores, computed for all pairs at once as a single matrix multiply.">
<rect x="110" y="460" width="166" height="44" rx="9" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="193" y="480" text-anchor="middle" class="scal-t" font-size="14.5">MatMul</text>
<text x="193" y="496" text-anchor="middle" class="scal-m" fill="#93c5fd" font-size="10.5">Q x K^T</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS2.SSS1" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Scale" data-tip="Divide every score by the square root of d_k. This is the only difference between this attention and plain dot-product attention, and it exists to keep the softmax out of its saturated region.">
<rect x="110" y="396" width="166" height="44" rx="9" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#f0883e" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="193" y="416" text-anchor="middle" class="scal-t" font-size="14.5">Scale</text>
<text x="193" y="432" text-anchor="middle" class="scal-m" fill="#f0883e" font-size="10.5">/ sqrt(d_k)</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS2.SSS3" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Mask, optional" data-tip="Used only in decoder self-attention. Every score that corresponds to an illegal connection is set to minus infinity here, before the softmax, so its weight comes out as exactly zero.">
<rect x="110" y="332" width="166" height="44" rx="9" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#f85149" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="6 4"/>
<text x="193" y="352" text-anchor="middle" class="scal-t" font-size="14.5">Mask (opt.)</text>
<text x="193" y="368" text-anchor="middle" class="scal-m" fill="#f85149" font-size="10.5">illegal = -inf</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.E1" target="_blank" data-tiphead="SoftMax" data-tip="Applied along each row, so the n scores for one query become n non-negative weights that sum to one. This is what makes attention a soft, differentiable lookup instead of a hard pick.">
<rect x="110" y="268" width="166" height="44" rx="9" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="193" y="288" text-anchor="middle" class="scal-t" font-size="14.5">SoftMax</text>
<text x="193" y="304" text-anchor="middle" class="scal-m" fill="#93c5fd" font-size="10.5">rows sum to 1</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.E1" target="_blank" data-tiphead="MatMul: weights times V" data-tip="The weighted sum. Output row i is the average of all value rows, weighted by row i of the softmax. The softmax couples the scores within a row, but only this product carries content from other positions into row i.">
<rect x="110" y="196" width="296" height="48" rx="9" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="258" y="218" text-anchor="middle" class="scal-t" font-size="14.5">MatMul</text>
<text x="258" y="235" text-anchor="middle" class="scal-m" fill="#93c5fd" font-size="10.5">weights x V</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS2.SSS2" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Head output" data-tip="One d_v-wide vector per position. Inside multi-head attention this is one of h such outputs, which are concatenated and projected back to 512 dimensions.">
<rect x="180" y="130" width="156" height="44" rx="9" fill="#0d1117" stroke="#93c5fd" stroke-width="1.8"/>
<text x="258" y="150" text-anchor="middle" class="scal-t" font-size="14.5">head output</text>
<text x="258" y="166" text-anchor="middle" class="scal-m" fill="#93c5fd" font-size="10.5">n x d_v</text>
</a>
<text x="470" y="176" class="scal-t" font-size="24">Attention(Q, K, V)</text>
<text x="726" y="176" class="scal-d" font-size="24">=</text>
<text x="758" y="176" fill="#3b82f6" font-size="24" font-weight="700">softmax</text>
<text x="862" y="182" class="scal-d" font-size="34">(</text>
<text x="936" y="162" text-anchor="middle" fill="#3fb950" font-size="22" font-weight="700">Q K</text>
<text x="960" y="152" fill="#3fb950" font-size="14" font-weight="700">T</text>
<path d="M894,172 L980,172" stroke="#a0a0a0" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="910" y="200" fill="#f0883e" font-size="24" font-weight="700">&#8730;</text>
<path d="M926,182 L958,182" stroke="#f0883e" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="928" y="200" fill="#f0883e" font-size="21" font-weight="700" font-style="italic">d</text>
<text x="942" y="205" fill="#f0883e" font-size="14" font-weight="700">k</text>
<text x="986" y="182" class="scal-d" font-size="34">)</text>
<text x="1016" y="176" fill="#bc8cff" font-size="24" font-weight="700" font-style="italic">V</text>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.E1" target="_blank"><text x="1136" y="176" text-anchor="end" class="scal-d" font-size="15">Eq. 1</text></a>
<text x="470" y="230" class="scal-d" font-size="12.5">Two matrix multiplies, one divide, one softmax. No recurrence, no convolution.</text>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.E1" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Q K transposed" data-tip="The compatibility function. Dot product rather than a small feed-forward network, because it can be run as one highly optimised matrix multiply.">
<rect x="450" y="268" width="690" height="64" rx="10" fill="#151515" stroke="#2a2a2a" stroke-width="1.4"/>
<text x="472" y="292" font-size="15"><tspan class="scal-m" fill="#3fb950" font-weight="700">Q K^T</tspan><tspan dx="18" fill="#f0f0f0">every query dotted with every key: an n x n table of raw scores</tspan></text>
<text x="472" y="316" class="scal-d" font-size="12.5">score[i][j] says how strongly position i wants to read from position j</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS2.SSS1" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Divide by the square root of d_k" data-tip="The scaling factor. It is the whole difference between this and classic dot-product attention, and the paper attributes it to the variance of the dot product growing with d_k.">
<rect x="450" y="344" width="690" height="64" rx="10" fill="#151515" stroke="#2a2a2a" stroke-width="1.4"/>
<text x="472" y="368" font-size="15"><tspan class="scal-m" fill="#f0883e" font-weight="700">/ sqrt(d_k)</tspan><tspan dx="18" fill="#f0f0f0">shrink the scores before the softmax sees them</tspan></text>
<text x="472" y="392" class="scal-d" font-size="12.5">d_k = 64 in the base model, so every score is divided by 8</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.E1" target="_blank" data-tiphead="softmax" data-tip="Applied row-wise. It converts scores into a distribution, which is what makes the read-out an average rather than a hard selection.">
<rect x="450" y="420" width="690" height="64" rx="10" fill="#151515" stroke="#2a2a2a" stroke-width="1.4"/>
<text x="472" y="444" font-size="15"><tspan class="scal-m" fill="#3b82f6" font-weight="700">softmax</tspan><tspan dx="18" fill="#f0f0f0">each row becomes a probability distribution over positions</tspan></text>
<text x="472" y="468" class="scal-d" font-size="12.5">the n weights in row i are non-negative and sum to 1: a soft, differentiable lookup</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS2" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Times V" data-tip="The read-out. The paper defines attention as a weighted sum of the values, where the weight on each value comes from the compatibility of the query with the matching key.">
<rect x="450" y="496" width="690" height="64" rx="10" fill="#151515" stroke="#2a2a2a" stroke-width="1.4"/>
<text x="472" y="520" font-size="15"><tspan class="scal-m" fill="#bc8cff" font-weight="700">x V</tspan><tspan dx="18" fill="#f0f0f0">the weights average the value rows: output row i is that average</tspan></text>
<text x="472" y="544" class="scal-d" font-size="12.5">softmax only reweights row i; this product is what copies other positions' content in</text>
</a>
</svg>
</div>

- **Dot product, not a small network**: <span class="term" data-tiphead="Additive attention" data-tip="The alternative compatibility function, from Bahdanau et al. 2014: a one-hidden-layer feed-forward network scoring the query against the key. Similar theoretical cost, much slower in practice.">additive attention</span> has similar theoretical cost, but the dot product runs as one optimised matrix multiply

---

<a class="slide-id" id="b20c0654-802f-4d2d-a4ff-1095b850a197"></a>

<!-- _class: fs-sm -->

## One attention sub-layer, end to end, with the shapes written out

| step | shape | with n = 10 tokens |
|---|---|---|
| layer input X | n × d_model | 10 × 512 |
| head i: X W<sub>i</sub><sup>Q</sup>, X W<sub>i</sub><sup>K</sup>, X W<sub>i</sub><sup>V</sup> (each W is 512 × 64) | n × d_k | 10 × 64 each |
| Q Kᵀ | n × n | 10 × 10 raw scores |
| ÷ √d_k, then softmax row-wise | n × n | each row sums to 1 |
| × V | n × d_v | 10 × 64 |
| concat 8 heads | n × h·d_v | 10 × 512 |
| × W<sup>O</sup> (512 × 512) | n × d_model | 10 × 512 |

- **n = 10 is illustrative**; `d_k = d_v = 64`, `d_model = 512` and `h = 8` are the paper's base model
- **Q Kᵀ only decides how much** to read; the multiply by **V** is where content from *other* positions enters row i
- **Encoder-decoder attention**: m target queries against n source keys give an **m × n** score matrix and an m × 512 output

---

<a class="slide-id" id="d271c1e1-6e9e-42cd-88c4-1e1896d318f9"></a>

<!-- _class: fs-sm -->

## Dividing by √d_k keeps the softmax out of the region where it has no gradient

<div style="display:flex;justify-content:center;margin-top:0.2rem">
<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 1160 600" width="780" height="404" style="max-width:100%" font-family="Inter, sans-serif">
<style>.sqrt-t{fill:#f0f0f0;font-weight:700}.sqrt-m{font-family:'JetBrains Mono',monospace}.sqrt-d{fill:#a0a0a0}</style>
<defs>
<marker id="ao" markerWidth="11" markerHeight="11" refX="8" refY="4" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L9,4 L0,8 z" fill="#f0883e"/></marker>
</defs>
<rect x="0" y="0" width="1160" height="600" fill="#111111"/>
<text x="580" y="52" text-anchor="middle" fill="#f0883e" font-size="16" font-weight="700">The argument for the scaling (paper footnote 4), step by step</text>
<path d="M280,135 L316,135" stroke="#f0883e" stroke-width="2.2" marker-end="url(#ao)" fill="none"/>
<path d="M570,135 L606,135" stroke="#f0883e" stroke-width="2.2" marker-end="url(#ao)" fill="none"/>
<path d="M860,135 L896,135" stroke="#f0883e" stroke-width="2.2" marker-end="url(#ao)" fill="none"/>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS2.SSS2" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Step 1: d_k grows" data-tip="d_k is the width of a single query or key vector. The base model uses 64 per head, but the ablation in Table 3 row A also runs a single head at the full 512.">
<rect x="30" y="80" width="250" height="110" rx="10" fill="#151515" stroke="#3a3a3a" stroke-width="1.5"/>
<text x="52" y="106" class="sqrt-t" font-size="14.5">d_k grows</text>
<text x="52" y="132" class="sqrt-d" font-size="11.5">queries and keys have d_k</text>
<text x="52" y="150" class="sqrt-d" font-size="11.5">components; 64 per head here,</text>
<text x="52" y="168" class="sqrt-d" font-size="11.5">but a full-width head uses 512.</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS2.SSS1" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Step 2: dot products grow" data-tip="Footnote 4 of the paper: if the components of q and k are independent with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has mean 0 and variance d_k. Typical magnitude therefore grows like the square root of d_k.">
<rect x="320" y="80" width="250" height="110" rx="10" fill="#151515" stroke="#3a3a3a" stroke-width="1.5"/>
<text x="342" y="106" class="sqrt-t" font-size="14.5">dot products grow</text>
<text x="342" y="132" class="sqrt-d" font-size="11.5">with mean-0, variance-1</text>
<text x="342" y="150" class="sqrt-d" font-size="11.5">components q . k has mean 0</text>
<text x="342" y="168" class="sqrt-d" font-size="11.5">and variance d_k.</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.E1" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Step 3: the softmax saturates" data-tip="Exponentiating scores that are tens of units apart makes one weight essentially 1 and the rest essentially 0. The row stops being a distribution over positions and becomes a hard pick.">
<rect x="610" y="80" width="250" height="110" rx="10" fill="#151515" stroke="#3a3a3a" stroke-width="1.5"/>
<text x="632" y="106" class="sqrt-t" font-size="14.5">the softmax saturates</text>
<text x="632" y="132" class="sqrt-d" font-size="11.5">one score dominates the row,</text>
<text x="632" y="150" class="sqrt-d" font-size="11.5">so the weights collapse onto</text>
<text x="632" y="168" class="sqrt-d" font-size="11.5">a single position.</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS2.SSS1" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Step 4: gradients vanish" data-tip="The paper suspects that for large d_k the dot products grow large in magnitude, pushing the softmax function into regions where it has extremely small gradients. That is the concrete failure being avoided.">
<rect x="900" y="80" width="250" height="110" rx="10" fill="#151515" stroke="#f85149" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="922" y="106" fill="#f85149" font-size="14.5" font-weight="700">gradients vanish</text>
<text x="922" y="132" class="sqrt-d" font-size="11.5">a saturated softmax has</text>
<text x="922" y="150" class="sqrt-d" font-size="11.5">extremely small gradients, so</text>
<text x="922" y="168" class="sqrt-d" font-size="11.5">the layer stops learning.</text>
</a>
<text x="330" y="282" text-anchor="middle" fill="#f0883e" font-size="13.5" font-weight="700">unscaled: softmax of the raw dot products</text>
<text x="830" y="282" text-anchor="middle" fill="#3b82f6" font-size="13.5" font-weight="700">scaled: same scores, each divided by 8</text>
<path d="M120,462 L560,462" stroke="#444" stroke-width="1.4"/>
<path d="M620,462 L1060,462" stroke="#444" stroke-width="1.4"/>
<text x="112" y="306" text-anchor="end" class="sqrt-d" font-size="11">1</text>
<text x="112" y="466" text-anchor="end" class="sqrt-d" font-size="11">0</text>
<text x="612" y="306" text-anchor="end" class="sqrt-d" font-size="11">1</text>
<text x="612" y="466" text-anchor="end" class="sqrt-d" font-size="11">0</text>
<rect x="150" y="302" width="56" height="158" rx="3" fill="#f0883e"/>
<rect x="226" y="454" width="56" height="6" rx="3" fill="#f0883e" opacity="0.55"/>
<rect x="302" y="454" width="56" height="6" rx="3" fill="#f0883e" opacity="0.55"/>
<rect x="378" y="454" width="56" height="6" rx="3" fill="#f0883e" opacity="0.55"/>
<rect x="454" y="454" width="56" height="6" rx="3" fill="#f0883e" opacity="0.55"/>
<rect x="650" y="362" width="56" height="98" rx="3" fill="#3b82f6"/>
<rect x="726" y="398" width="56" height="62" rx="3" fill="#3b82f6" opacity="0.85"/>
<rect x="802" y="420" width="56" height="40" rx="3" fill="#3b82f6" opacity="0.7"/>
<rect x="878" y="434" width="56" height="26" rx="3" fill="#3b82f6" opacity="0.55"/>
<rect x="954" y="444" width="56" height="16" rx="3" fill="#3b82f6" opacity="0.4"/>
<text x="330" y="486" text-anchor="middle" class="sqrt-d" font-size="11.5">one weight near 1, the rest near 0 - almost no gradient</text>
<text x="830" y="486" text-anchor="middle" class="sqrt-d" font-size="11.5">a usable spread of weights - gradient still flows</text>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS2.SSS1" target="_blank" data-tiphead="The fix" data-tip="Dividing by the square root of d_k is the only difference between scaled dot-product attention and the classic dot-product attention it is built on.">
<rect x="30" y="500" width="1100" height="72" rx="10" fill="#0d1117" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="1.8"/>
<text x="52" y="528" class="sqrt-t" font-size="14.5">The fix: divide every score by sqrt(d_k) before the softmax. With d_k = 64 that is a division by 8.</text>
<text x="52" y="554" class="sqrt-d" font-size="12.5">Britz et al. (2017), a large sweep of translation architectures: additive attention outperforms dot-product without scaling at large d_k.</text>
</a>
<text x="1130" y="252" text-anchor="end" fill="#f0883e" font-size="11.5">bar heights illustrative</text>
</svg>
</div>

- **Thin evidence**: footnote 4 assumes **independent, mean-0, variance-1** q and k components; the cited result, [Britz et al. 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.03906), a large sweep of translation models, found additive attention beating *unscaled* dot product at large d_k. **No Table 3 row** drops the scaling or learns it
- **Our numbers**: at d_k = 64 two scores differ by about 8·√2 ≈ 11, so a gap of 16 is ordinary: weights e¹⁶ ≈ 9 million to 1; divided by 8, e² ≈ 7 to 1

<text x="375" y="484" text-anchor="middle" class="mult-t" font-size="14">Linear</text>

</a>

<text x="110" y="396" text-anchor="middle" class="mult-t" font-size="13.5">head 1</text>

</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS2.SSS1" target="_blank" data-tiphead="One head" data-tip="Heads run in parallel and never see each other until the concatenation, so they can specialise. Figure 5 of the paper shows heads whose behaviour seems related to the structure of the sentence.">
<rect x="185" y="374" width="120" height="58" rx="9" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="245" y="396" text-anchor="middle" class="mult-t" font-size="13.5">head 2</text>
<text x="245" y="416" text-anchor="middle" class="mult-m" fill="#93c5fd" font-size="10">d_k = 64</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS2.SSS2" target="_blank" data-tiphead="One head" data-tip="The base model uses h = 8. Table 3 row A varies h from 1 to 32 at constant compute and finds 8 and 16 best.">
<rect x="350" y="374" width="120" height="58" rx="9" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="410" y="396" text-anchor="middle" class="mult-t" font-size="13.5">head 8</text>
<text x="410" y="416" text-anchor="middle" class="mult-m" fill="#93c5fd" font-size="10">d_k = 64</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS2.SSS2" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Concat" data-tip="The h head outputs of width d_v are laid side by side, giving h times d_v = 512 columns again.">
<rect x="50" y="292" width="420" height="48" rx="9" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="260" y="312" text-anchor="middle" class="mult-t" font-size="14.5">Concat</text>
<text x="260" y="329" text-anchor="middle" class="mult-m" fill="#93c5fd" font-size="10.5">8 x 64 = 512 columns</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS2.SSS2" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Output projection W^O" data-tip="A final learned 512-by-512 matrix that mixes the concatenated heads back into one representation. Without it the heads would remain in disjoint slices of the vector.">
<rect x="140" y="214" width="240" height="48" rx="9" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="260" y="234" text-anchor="middle" class="mult-t" font-size="14.5">Linear</text>
<text x="260" y="251" text-anchor="middle" class="mult-m" fill="#93c5fd" font-size="10.5">W^O, 512 to 512</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS1" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Sub-layer output" data-tip="512 dimensions per position, the same width as every other sub-layer output and every embedding, so the residual addition always lines up.">
<rect x="140" y="142" width="240" height="48" rx="9" fill="#0d1117" stroke="#93c5fd" stroke-width="1.8"/>
<text x="260" y="162" text-anchor="middle" class="mult-t" font-size="14.5">sub-layer output</text>
<text x="260" y="179" text-anchor="middle" class="mult-m" fill="#93c5fd" font-size="10.5">n x 512</text>
</a>
<text x="560" y="108" class="mult-t" font-size="17">MultiHead(Q, K, V) = Concat(head_1, ..., head_h) W^O</text>
<text x="560" y="140" class="mult-d" font-size="17">where head_i = Attention(Q W_i^Q, K W_i^K, V W_i^V)</text>
<text x="560" y="170" class="mult-d" font-size="13">Here Q, K, V are the raw inputs X, Y, Y: each is projected once, per head.</text>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS2.SSS2" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Why the cost stays flat" data-tip="Because each head is narrower by exactly the factor h, the total work across all heads is about the work of one full-width head. The paper states the total computational cost is similar to that of single-head attention with full dimensionality.">
<rect x="560" y="188" width="580" height="134" rx="10" fill="#151515" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="582" y="214" fill="#3b82f6" font-size="14.5" font-weight="700">Eight heads cost about one full-width head</text>
<text x="582" y="242" class="mult-d" font-size="13">h = 8 heads, each d_k = d_v = 512 / 8 = 64. Equal in two senses:</text>
<text x="582" y="264" class="mult-d" font-size="13">weights: eight 512 x 64 projections per input = one 512 x 512;</text>
<text x="582" y="286" class="mult-d" font-size="13">score FLOPs: eight products Q_i K_i^T at width 64 = one at 512.</text>
<text x="582" y="308" class="mult-d" font-size="13">Not equal: 8 softmaxes and 8 n x n weight matrices instead of 1.</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS2.SSS2" target="_blank" data-tiphead="What the extra heads buy" data-tip="Multi-head attention lets the model jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions. With a single attention head, averaging inhibits this.">
<rect x="560" y="338" width="580" height="112" rx="10" fill="#151515" stroke="#2a2a2a" stroke-width="1.4"/>
<text x="582" y="364" class="mult-t" font-size="14.5">What the extra heads buy (example illustrative)</text>
<text x="582" y="392" class="mult-d" font-size="13">A verb needs its subject and its object. One head gives one</text>
<text x="582" y="414" class="mult-d" font-size="13">weighted average, so a 50/50 split returns a blur of both words.</text>
<text x="582" y="436" class="mult-d" font-size="13">Two heads can each take one, kept apart in separate concat slices.</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S6.T3" target="_blank" data-tiphead="What the ablation shows" data-tip="Table 3 rows A vary the number of heads while keeping the amount of computation constant. Single-head attention is 0.9 BLEU worse than the best setting, and quality also drops off with too many heads.">
<rect x="560" y="466" width="580" height="112" rx="10" fill="#151515" stroke="#2a2a2a" stroke-width="1.4"/>
<text x="582" y="492" class="mult-t" font-size="14.5">What the ablation shows (Table 3, rows A)</text>
<text x="582" y="520" class="mult-d" font-size="13">Compute held constant, h varied: h = 1 gives 24.9 BLEU,</text>
<text x="582" y="542" class="mult-d" font-size="13">h = 8 gives 25.8, h = 16 also 25.8, h = 32 drops to 25.4.</text>
<text x="582" y="564" class="mult-d" font-size="13">Not monotonic; and h = 1 also widens d_k to 512, two changes at once.</text>
</a>
</svg>
</div>

---

<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS2.SSS3" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Where the mask lands" data-tip="Section 3.2.3 places the mask inside scaled dot-product attention, on the input of the softmax. That placement is what makes the zeros exact rather than merely small.">
<rect x="60" y="390" width="1040" height="176" rx="10" fill="#0d1117" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="1.8"/>
<text x="84" y="420" class="mask-t" font-size="15">Exactly what is set to minus infinity, and exactly where</text>
<text x="84" y="448" class="mask-d" font-size="13.5">Section 3.2.3: the mask is applied inside scaled dot-product attention, to all values in the input of the</text>
<text x="84" y="470" class="mask-d" font-size="13.5">softmax which correspond to illegal connections. Illegal means every pair where j is greater than i.</text>
<text x="84" y="498" class="mask-d" font-size="13">Because the mask hits the scores and not the outputs, the softmax turns those cells into exact zeros:</text>
<text x="84" y="520" class="mask-d" font-size="13">no value from a future token is summed in, and no gradient flows backwards in time through them.</text>
<text x="84" y="548" class="mask-d" font-size="13">Together with the output embedding being offset by one position, this is what keeps the decoder autoregressive.</text>
</a>
</svg>
</div>

- §3.2.3 masks every pair with **j &gt; i** in "the input of the softmax", so the weights are **exactly zero**; j = i is safe, as input i holds token i−1 (slide 9)
- **This one mask suffices**: feed-forward, residual and LayerNorm act per position, and encoder-decoder attention reads only the source, so no other path joins two target positions

<text x="200" y="460" text-anchor="middle" class="subl-t" font-size="14.5">Sublayer(x)</text>
<text x="200" y="480" text-anchor="middle" class="subl-d" font-size="11.5">attention or feed-forward</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS1" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Layer normalisation" data-tip="The paper writes the whole wrapper as LayerNorm of x plus Sublayer of x. Note the ordering: the norm comes after the addition, which is the post-norm arrangement.">
<rect x="50" y="318" width="300" height="46" rx="9" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="200" y="347" text-anchor="middle" class="subl-t" font-size="14.5">LayerNorm</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS1" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Sub-layer output" data-tip="Fed straight into the next sub-layer. Six such layers on the encoder side, six on the decoder side.">

<text x="200" y="272" text-anchor="middle" class="subl-m subl-t" font-size="13">output</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS1" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Why the shapes always line up" data-tip="To facilitate the residual connections, all sub-layers in the model as well as the embedding layers produce outputs of dimension 512.">
<rect x="20" y="110" width="360" height="110" rx="10" fill="#151515" stroke="#2a2a2a" stroke-width="1.4"/>
<text x="42" y="136" class="subl-t" font-size="13.5">Why the shapes always line up</text>
<text x="42" y="162" class="subl-d" font-size="11.5">Every sub-layer and every embedding</text>
<text x="42" y="182" class="subl-d" font-size="11.5">layer emits 512 dimensions, so x and</text>
<text x="42" y="202" class="subl-d" font-size="11.5">Sublayer(x) can always be added.</text>
</a>
<text x="415" y="102" class="subl-m" fill="#f0f0f0" font-size="13.5">FFN(x) = max(0, x W1 + b1) W2 + b2</text>
<path d="M580,512 L580,494" stroke="#3fb950" stroke-width="2.2" marker-end="url(#ag)" fill="none"/>
<path d="M580,430 L580,396" stroke="#3fb950" stroke-width="2.2" marker-end="url(#ag)" fill="none"/>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS3" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Input to the feed-forward net" data-tip="One 512-dimensional vector per position, taken from the attention sub-layer below.">
<rect x="450" y="512" width="260" height="40" rx="8" fill="#0d1117" stroke="#2a2a2a" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="580" y="538" text-anchor="middle" class="subl-d" font-size="12.5">input: 512 per position</text>
</a>

<rect x="450" y="430" width="260" height="56" rx="9" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#3fb950" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="580" y="454" text-anchor="middle" class="subl-t" font-size="14.5">Linear to 2048</text>
<text x="580" y="474" text-anchor="middle" class="subl-d" font-size="11.5">then ReLU</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.E2" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Output layer" data-tip="A second linear map back down to 512, so the result can go through the residual addition unchanged in shape.">
<rect x="450" y="348" width="260" height="40" rx="8" fill="#1a1a1a" stroke="#3fb950" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="580" y="374" text-anchor="middle" class="subl-t" font-size="13.5">Linear back to 512</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS3" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Three things people skip" data-tip="The feed-forward network is where each position digests what it just read; nothing here moves information between positions. That job belongs entirely to attention.">
<rect x="400" y="130" width="360" height="170" rx="10" fill="#151515" stroke="#2a2a2a" stroke-width="1.4"/>
<text x="422" y="156" class="subl-t" font-size="13.5">Three things worth noticing</text>
<text x="422" y="180" class="subl-d" font-size="11.5">Applied to each position separately</text>
<text x="422" y="200" class="subl-d" font-size="11.5">and identically: nothing mixes across</text>
<text x="422" y="220" class="subl-d" font-size="11.5">positions here, only attention does.</text>
<text x="422" y="244" class="subl-d" font-size="11.5">Same weights across positions in one</text>
<text x="422" y="264" class="subl-d" font-size="11.5">layer, different weights per layer.</text>
<text x="422" y="288" class="subl-d" font-size="11.5">Equivalently two convolutions, kernel 1.</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S3.SS4" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Shared embedding weights" data-tip="The same weight matrix is shared between the two embedding layers and the pre-softmax linear transformation, and in the embedding layers those weights are multiplied by the square root of d_model. Sharing one matrix between input and output embeddings needs one vocabulary for both languages: the paper states a shared source-target vocabulary for English-German, and only a 32000 word-piece vocabulary for English-French. It gives no reason for the square-root scaling.">
<rect x="780" y="100" width="360" height="170" rx="10" fill="#151515" stroke="#3d2f52" stroke-width="1.6"/>
<text x="802" y="126" fill="#bc8cff" font-size="13.5" font-weight="700">Shared embedding weights</text>
<text x="802" y="150" class="subl-d" font-size="11.5">One matrix serves the input embedding,</text>
<text x="802" y="168" class="subl-d" font-size="11.5">the output embedding and the linear layer</text>
<text x="802" y="186" class="subl-d" font-size="11.5">before the softmax, so source and target</text>
<text x="802" y="204" class="subl-d" font-size="11.5">must share one vocabulary: the paper says</text>
<text x="802" y="222" class="subl-d" font-size="11.5">so for En-De (37000 BPE tokens), not for</text>
<text x="802" y="240" class="subl-d" font-size="11.5">En-Fr. In the embeddings the weights are</text>
<text x="802" y="258" class="subl-d" font-size="11.5">multiplied by sqrt(512), about 22.6.</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S5.SS4" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Where dropout is applied" data-tip="Dropout is applied to the output of each sub-layer before it is added to the sub-layer input and normalised, and to the sums of the embeddings and the positional encodings in both stacks.">
<rect x="780" y="290" width="360" height="170" rx="10" fill="#151515" stroke="#2a2a2a" stroke-width="1.4"/>
<text x="802" y="316" class="subl-t" font-size="13.5">Where dropout is applied</text>
<text x="802" y="342" class="subl-d" font-size="11.5">To the output of every sub-layer, before</text>
<text x="802" y="362" class="subl-d" font-size="11.5">it is added to the sub-layer input and</text>
<text x="802" y="382" class="subl-d" font-size="11.5">normalised.</text>
<text x="802" y="408" class="subl-d" font-size="11.5">Also to the sums of the embeddings and</text>
<text x="802" y="428" class="subl-d" font-size="11.5">the positional encodings in both stacks.</text>
<text x="802" y="448" class="subl-d" font-size="11.5">Rate 0.1 for base, 0.3 for the big model.</text>
</a>
<a href="https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1706.03762#S6.T3" target="_blank" data-tiphead="Base model shape" data-tip="The base configuration is the top row of Table 3: 6 layers, d_model 512, d_ff 2048, 8 heads, 65 million parameters.">
<rect x="780" y="480" width="360" height="96" rx="10" fill="#0d1117" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="1.6"/>

<text x="60" y="314" text-anchor="end" class="pose-d" font-size="11">0</text>
